bodyText: The hardest part of the first days is not knowing what you don't know yet. That gets easier faster than you think. Your baby has been listening to your voice for months. She already knows you.
She will sleep most of the time, and wake to eat, and sleep again. That is the whole job right now — hers and yours. Don't count the hours. Just feed her when she asks and let everything else wait.

Babies cry differently for different things, and you will learn the difference between hunger and discomfort and just needing to be held. You'll know sooner than you expect. Right now it all sounds the same because it's all new.

Back to sleep, every time. On his back, on a firm flat surface with nothing else in the crib — no blankets, no bumpers, no stuffed animals. That's the one rule in these first weeks that I'd ask you to follow without exception.

Hold him as much as you want. You can't spoil a newborn with holding. What you're doing when you hold him and talk to him is teaching him that the world is a place worth being in. That's not a small thing.

Your baby can see your face clearly from about the distance you hold her when you feed her. She is looking at you. Look back. She is learning faces, and yours is the most important one she'll ever learn.
The end of the first week is a good time to just breathe. You kept a person alive for seven days. That's what you did. Whatever else didn't happen doesn't count right now.

Talk to him. Narrate whatever you're doing — changing him, carrying him, looking out the window. He can't understand the words yet, but he's building the architecture of language every time he hears your voice. The talking matters.

She may have days where she feeds constantly and nothing seems to satisfy her. Growth spurts do this, and they pass. Feed her on demand. Your body — if you're breastfeeding — will catch up. Trust the system even when it doesn't feel like it's working.

You're going to get contradictory advice from people who love you. Take what fits and let the rest go. The people offering it mean well. But they're not in your house at two in the morning, and you are.

Skin-to-skin time in these first weeks does things that are hard to measure but real — warmth, regulation, the beginning of a bond that will outlast everything. Even a few minutes of it, when you can manage it, is worth having.
If you're the one who carried this baby, your body went through something significant. Pay attention to how you're feeling, not just how the baby is feeling. You matter in this equation too.

Tummy time starts now, even at a week old. A few minutes at a time while the baby is awake and you're watching. It strengthens the neck and shoulders he'll need to lift his head — which he'll start doing soon, and which will feel like a miracle when he does.

Two weeks in. You've figured out more than you realize. The chaos is real, but underneath it something is being built between you and this baby that doesn't show up on a schedule or a checklist. It's already there.

Around now she'll start to follow your face with her eyes when you move slowly in front of her. She's not just looking — she's tracking. That's her brain doing something new. Give her something worth following.

He can hear you clearly. He's been able to since before he was born. Singing to him, talking to him, even just humming while you move around the room — all of it lands. He turns toward sound. He's listening for you specifically.

Tummy time is going to feel like a big deal to her. She may not like it. Do it anyway, in short stretches, while you're right there with her. She needs to build those neck muscles and she can't do it on her back.

Sleep is not something you can fix right now, and trying to fix it will wear you out faster than the sleep deprivation itself. You are in the thick of it. This is genuinely the hardest phase. It does not last.
When she cries and you pick her up, you are not teaching her that crying is a strategy. You are teaching her that the world responds to her. That's exactly what she needs to learn at one month old.

His personality is already in there. You can see it — which sounds seem to calm him, which positions he prefers, whether he'd rather look around or look at your face. Pay attention to what you're learning about him specifically.
Make sure she gets outside at some point, even briefly. Fresh air and a change of light and sound is good for both of you. Nothing dramatic. Just out and back.

Around now, some babies start to settle into a loose pattern of sleeping more at night than during the day. Not a schedule — just a drift. When you see it starting, follow his lead and encourage the drift. Don't force it.
If you have other children, they are watching how you are with the baby and learning from it. What you're modeling — gentleness, patience, attention — they are absorbing. Even on the hard days.

At a month, she can briefly lift her head when she's on her tummy. You might not notice it happening, and then one day you'll see her do it and it'll feel significant. It is. That's real physical strength she just earned.

He coos. It doesn't sound like much but it's the beginning of everything — the earliest attempt at communication that isn't just crying. When he does it, respond. Talk back. Make it a conversation even if only one of you has words.
Feeding on demand in these early weeks is not a habit to break later. It's how milk supply regulates and how her appetite calibrates. The schedules can wait. Right now, feed when she's hungry.

You may notice that she's more alert at certain times of day than others. Start to learn her alert windows — those are the best times for tummy time, for talking to her, for the few minutes of play that count as play right now.
It is okay to put him down in a safe place and walk away for a few minutes. A crying baby who is safe is less dangerous than a parent who is at the end of their rope. Take the break when you need it.

She may have evenings where she fusses for hours and nothing helps. Some babies just do this. You haven't done anything wrong. It's not reflux or hunger or pain — sometimes it's just what evenings look like for a while. It passes.
Keep a loose log of wet diapers if you're breastfeeding and wondering whether she's getting enough. Six wet diapers a day is the reassuring number. You don't need a scale — you need that number.
He's starting to recognize the difference between your voice and other voices. You are not just familiar — you are already his person. That happened fast.

Reading to her at one month feels a little absurd. Read anyway. The words don't matter. Your voice matters. The rhythm of language matters. The habit of sitting quietly together with a book matters more than you'd think.

Ask for help before you need it desperately. The people who want to help you are waiting to be told what to do. Give them a specific job — meals, laundry, sitting with the baby while you sleep for two hours. Specific is easier than general.

He may start to show you something that looks almost like a smile around now. It's not gas — it's the beginning of a social smile, which is one of the things that makes the first weeks start to feel worth it.

Pacifiers, if you use them, don't cause nipple confusion when breastfeeding is established. They may reduce SIDS risk. Use them if they help. Don't use them if they don't. There's no wrong answer here.
The way you feel about yourself as a parent has very little to do with how good a parent you actually are right now. Doubt is not evidence. You're doing this, which is the only thing that counts.

She's going to have nights that are worse than the ones before. That's not backsliding — that's just how the first months go. Growth spurts, developmental leaps, nothing you did. Worse nights happen and then things settle again.
The bath doesn't have to happen every day. Once or twice a week is enough. What your baby needs more than cleanliness is warm water and your hands and the closeness of it. The rest is logistics.

When he's on your chest listening to your heartbeat, he's doing something he's been doing since before he was born. You are a familiar place. That matters more than anything you could engineer or optimize.

She's starting to track moving objects with her eyes — not just faces now, but things that move across her field of vision. A mobile above her, your hand moving slowly, light and shadow. Her visual world is opening up.

If you're feeling something heavier than tired — not just exhausted but flat, or detached, or weeping in ways that don't make sense — say something to someone. To your doctor, to your partner, to anyone. That feeling has a name and it has a treatment and you don't have to manage it alone.
He doesn't need a lot of toys right now. He needs your face, your voice, contrast (black and white patterns, faces, light and shadow), and tummy time. The rest is marketing.

One month in, your baby is bigger and more alert than she was at birth. She looks at you differently. You look at her differently. Something is already established between you that wasn't there four weeks ago. That's real, even when the days are very hard.
The first month is the hardest one. You made it through it. That's not nothing.
The social smile is real now — not just a flicker but a full response, directed at you, when you talk to her or catch her eye. It's one of the better moments in the first year. Let yourself feel it.

He's cooing. Those soft sounds he makes when you talk to him are not random — they're his side of a conversation. Copy him back. Pause and wait. He'll try again. That back-and-forth is how language begins.

She can hold her head up for a few seconds when she's on her tummy now. That took real work. It doesn't look like much but those neck muscles are the beginning of sitting, which is the beginning of everything that comes after.

Two-month vaccines are coming up. What you may notice afterward: a sore leg where the shots went in, fussiness, a low fever, more sleeping than usual. All of that is normal and temporary. Cold cloth on the leg, extra holding, and time.
He's starting to recognize you from across the room — not just by voice anymore but by sight. He'll track your face when you move. You're becoming his landmark.

She may start to bring her hands to her mouth. This is self-soothing — her first independent attempt at calming herself. Let her do it. She's not teaching herself a bad habit. She's figuring out that her body has resources.
Tummy time is getting more useful now. He'll push up a little on his forearms. Put a rolled towel under his chest if he needs help. Get down on the floor at his level. Make eye contact. It helps.

Talk to her about what you're seeing. Not performing — just narrating. 'That's a tree. The branches are moving.' She can't understand yet, but the quantity and variety of words she hears now will matter later in ways you can measure.

His cries are starting to differentiate. Hunger sounds different from overtired sounds different from pain sounds different from wanting-to-be-held sounds. You may not be able to name them yet but you're already reading them. Trust what you notice.
She sleeps a lot and she still should. Sleep is when most of the brain development happens right now. Let her sleep.

A routine isn't a schedule — it doesn't have to happen at exact times. It's a sequence: feed, play a little, sleep. When the sequence becomes familiar, the baby starts to anticipate what comes next. That predictability is calming for both of you.

He's looking at faces more than anything else. Human faces are the most interesting thing in his world right now. Let him look at yours. Exaggerate your expressions — big smiles, wide eyes. He'll mimic them back. It's not silly. It's neuroscience.

The evenings may still be rough. Some babies have a fussy period every day around the same time, usually late afternoon or early evening, and there's not much that helps except holding them and waiting it out. It usually peaks around six weeks and then eases. If you're past that, it's almost over.
She can follow something moving slowly in front of her with her eyes — left to right, then back. She's paying attention. What you're seeing is concentration. It's already its own thing.
You're two months in. The part where you didn't know anything is behind you. You still have more to learn but you're not starting from zero anymore.

Peek-a-boo starts now. She won't understand it the way a six-month-old will, but the moment of your face appearing — the surprise of it — registers. Do it gently. It's one of the oldest games there is for a reason.
He's starting to look around when something makes a sound. He turns his head toward the source. That's hearing and attention and intention working together. It just started.
If you're breastfeeding and going back to work, now is the time to start thinking about pumping and introducing a bottle — before you actually need to. The transition is easier if it's not rushed.

She may start to show boredom. She'll look away, fuss a little, want something to change. That's a new thing — an opinion about her environment. It means her brain is asking for more than it was a few weeks ago.

Singing to him is doing something. The rhythm and repetition of songs are scaffolding for the way language and memory will develop. It doesn't matter if you can't carry a tune. He doesn't know that yet.
She's strong enough now that holding her upright with her feet pressed against your legs feels different than it did a month ago. She pushes. Her legs are already doing something.

The two-month visit with your pediatrician is a good one to come to with questions. Write them down. Not because you'll forget — you will — but because the act of writing helps you figure out which things are actually bothering you.
He will cry and you will try everything and nothing will work and eventually he'll stop. On those nights, you haven't failed at anything. Some crying doesn't have a solution. It just has an end.

She'll go through phases where she nurses constantly for a day or two. It looks like a supply problem but it's usually a growth spurt — her way of asking your body to make more milk. Feed on demand through it and the supply catches up.
He's starting to make arm and leg movements that are smoother than they were at birth. Less startling. More intentional. His nervous system is maturing in ways you can actually see.
This is around when some parents start to feel something other than survival. Not joy exactly — more like the beginning of recognition. You're starting to know each other.

If you have a partner, they matter in this too — and the baby knows them now. The more time a partner spends doing the actual caregiving, the more the baby orients to them. It takes time and repetition, same as anything.

She responds to your voice differently than to other voices now. You've been the most consistent sound in her world since before she was born. That means something to her brain even if she can't show you what.
The black-and-white high-contrast stuff that seemed interesting for a while is starting to give way. She wants color now, and faces, and movement. Her visual world is filling in.
Two months. The hardest part is behind you, even if it doesn't feel that way. What comes next is harder in some ways and better in many others.
He laughs now. Or something very close to a laugh — a squeal, a giggle, a sound that is unmistakably delight. Chase that sound. Do whatever made it happen again. You just found something.

She's reaching for things she sees. Her hands are starting to close around objects she didn't intend to pick up a few weeks ago. That's coordination arriving. Give her things to reach toward — not toys necessarily, just your fingers.

He holds his head steady now. Not perfectly, not always, but well enough that you're starting to carry him facing out, and he is looking at the world with great interest. Let him look. Point things out.

At three months, babies start to have more predictable stretches of sleep at night — not a full night, but longer than before. If you see a five-hour stretch, it's real. It's not a fluke. Protect that anchor sleep.

She's starting to recognize her name. Not to respond to it consistently yet — that comes later — but something in her changes when she hears it. Use it. Say it. Let her name become something familiar.
Tummy time is more interesting now because he's stronger. He can push up on his forearms and look around. Get toys at his eye level on the floor. Make the view worth the effort.

She's watching what you do with your hands. She's building a map of how hands work. Slow, deliberate hand movements in front of her — picking things up, pointing, waving — are more educational than anything you'd buy.

He may start to prefer you over other people in a way that wasn't obvious before. Not separation anxiety yet — that comes later — but a preference, a settling when he's in your arms versus anyone else's. You've been earned.

Baths might actually be enjoyable for her now. She's big enough to feel the water differently. Splash with her. Let it be slower and less efficient than it needs to be. She's not going to remember it, but you might.
His hands are open more than they're clenched now. He'll bring them together in front of him and look at them like they're something he just discovered, which they are.

Read to her every day even though she can't understand a word. The habit of reading together — the closeness, the sound of your voice, the rhythm of sentences — is worth building before comprehension catches up to it.

He's starting to understand cause and effect at the most basic level. He kicks and the mobile moves. He cries and you appear. He shakes something and it makes noise. He is building a model of how the world works.
Around three months, some parents hit a wall. The newborn intensity fades but the baby isn't yet interactive in the ways that feel rewarding. It can feel flat. That's a real phase. It passes.

She may try to roll front to back this month. She'll work at it for a while before she gets it, and when she does, she'll look startled that it worked. Be ready for it — she'll need a clear surface around her.

Mirror time. A baby-safe mirror near his play area, or held so he can see himself — he'll look for a long time. He doesn't know it's him yet, but he's fascinated. That's fine. So is the face he's looking at.

She can copy facial expressions now — not perfectly, but she'll try. Stick out your tongue slowly. Wait. Try again. She may do it back. That's imitation, which is the beginning of learning everything she will ever learn from watching people.
He may be sleeping in 4–6 hour stretches some nights. That is not a coincidence or luck. His sleep architecture is actually organizing itself. He's doing the work. You just have to not interrupt it.

She babbles in longer strings now — vowel sounds that go on and on. She's practicing the music of language before she has any of the words. Listen to it. She'll pause and look at you waiting for a response.
He pushes on your hands with his feet when you hold him standing. He's not ready to stand — not even close — but his legs are doing something they want to do and you can feel the strength in them.

If you're heading back to work soon, the anticipatory guilt is real and worth naming. It doesn't mean something is wrong with how you feel about your baby. It means you love them and you have to do this anyway. Both things are true.
She'll track a toy moving across her field of vision from side to side now. Hold something colorful about 8–10 inches from her face and move it slowly. Watch her eyes.
He knows your smell. He will orient toward you in a room. That recognition runs deep — it was built in the weeks before you even met each other.
Three months is when a lot of the colicky, high-cry evenings start to ease. Not for everyone, and not overnight, but this is around the corner. If you're still in it, you're near the other side.

She watches your mouth when you talk to her. She's studying the mechanics of speech — not the words, but the shapes your mouth makes to produce them. That is early language acquisition, and it's already happening.

He'll hold a toy briefly now if you put it in his hand — a rattle, a ring, something with texture. He'll look at it. He'll probably put it in his mouth. That's fine. That's what mouths are for, at three months.

One hundred days with this baby. That number is probably not one you've been counting, but it's worth sitting with. A hundred days ago you hadn't met each other. Now you know each other better than most people will.
She may be growing so fast right now that you notice it week to week. That rate of growth won't last — it never does — but it's remarkable while it's happening.

He makes sounds that feel like answers to things you've said. He can't be answering — he doesn't have the language — but the timing is there, the turn-taking is there, and that's the form of conversation before there are any words in it.
She's more interested in the world than she was a month ago. New rooms, new light, new sounds — she turns toward them. She's curious. That curiosity is one of the most important things she has.

Three months is a corner. Things get easier from here in some ways — not easier exactly, but different. More responsive. More interesting. The baby you're going to have a relationship with is starting to show up.

Four months is when most babies go through a sleep change that feels like a regression. It isn't going backward — it's the sleep cycle maturing. The naps get shorter, the nights get worse for a while. Knowing it's developmental doesn't make it less exhausting. It does make it less alarming.
She spontaneously smiles at people now — not just you, but faces she finds interesting. She's becoming social. That's a new thing about her that wasn't there a month ago.
He may roll front to back this month, if he hasn't already. When he does, he'll look surprised. The ground he was just on is not where he expected to end up. Give him a clear space to roll into.
She can hold her head steady and move it toward sounds, toward you, toward things she wants to look at. That head control is what's going to allow sitting, eventually. She's building the scaffolding.

He babbles with expression now — not just sounds but sounds with feeling in them, sounds that go up at the end like questions, sounds that repeat like insistence. He's telling you things. Listen as if they're words.
She reaches for things and actually gets them more often now. Her grip is getting better. She'll grab your hair, your glasses, whatever's within reach. This is coordination improving in real time.
Four-month vaccines happen at this visit. Same as two months: expect fussiness, a sore leg, possibly a low fever, more sleep than usual. All temporary. A cold cloth on the injection site helps.
He's starting to show interest in his own hands like they're separate things — examining them, bringing them together, watching his fingers move. He's discovering he has a body, piece by piece.
She may push up on her hands during tummy time now, not just her forearms. Her chest is coming up off the floor. That's real upper body strength. It's coming faster than you might expect.

He cries differently for different things now in ways that are becoming legible to you. You know his cries. That knowledge was built over four months of paying attention at two in the morning. It doesn't feel like expertise but it is.

She may be starting to show what her personality is going to be. Some babies are watchful. Some are physical. Some want to be held constantly. Some want to be put down and given space. She's showing you who she is. Pay attention.
He can bear weight on his legs when you hold him standing. He'll bounce. He likes it. Those leg muscles are starting to mean something. Don't force it — just let him push when he wants to.
She can track something moving in a full arc now — up, across, down. Her visual tracking is sophisticated enough to follow a face walking across a room. She's watching everything.

At this age, babies are starting to understand that objects exist even when they can't see them — very early object permanence. Hide a toy slowly under a blanket while he watches. He may look for it. That's a new thought he just had.

Solid food comes up a lot around four months. The recommendation from your pediatrician is probably to wait until six months unless there's a specific reason not to. Ask at the four-month visit. Don't rush it on your own.
She laughs at specific things now — at your face, at a silly sound, at something she's decided is funny. That specificity is new. Her sense of what's interesting is becoming her own.
He may start to grab his feet when he's on his back. This is a significant development — his body awareness is extending. He's learning he has legs. Next comes trying to put them in his mouth.
Keep reading to her, even though she's more interested in grabbing the book than listening to it. Let her grab the book. The handling of books is part of learning what books are.

He may be trying to get places. Not crawling yet, but the intention is there — pushing backward, rolling toward things he wants. He's frustrated when the toy is out of reach. That frustration is the beginning of motivation.

She'll watch intently when you eat. She may reach for what you're having. This is normal — she's not ready yet, but her interest is a sign that readiness is coming. Don't ignore the interest; just don't rush past the readiness markers either.

He's copying you. Facial expressions especially — you frown, he frowns. You open your eyes wide, he opens his eyes wide. He's learning the vocabulary of faces by imitating yours. You are his curriculum.

The bath is a legitimate activity now, not just hygiene. She splashes. She kicks. She has opinions about the temperature and the speed. Some evenings the bath is the thing that turns a hard hour around.

He may have a favorite toy now — not necessarily something you bought, possibly something boring like a wooden spoon or a piece of fabric — and he'll look for it if it disappears. That preference is him having an opinion, which is a whole new thing.

She passes things from one hand to the other this month — or starts to. Watch for it. It doesn't look like much but it requires the two sides of her brain to coordinate, which is not something she could do four weeks ago.
Four months is also when some parents feel a kind of grief for the very early days — even though those days were brutal. There's something that ends around now. It's okay to notice that.

He's making consonant sounds now — ba, ma, da — not directed at anyone in particular, just practicing. When he says 'dada' at four months, he doesn't mean his father. He means he learned to make that sound. The meaning comes later.

She has strong opinions about what she wants and she has more ways to communicate them now. A baby who three months ago had one mode of expression — crying — now has sounds, faces, reaching, turning away, engaging. She's talking to you.

The night waking is hard. The fourth month is often the hardest stretch of sleep in the whole first year for parents. It doesn't mean anything is wrong. It means you're exactly where you're supposed to be.
He knows people he sees regularly. He has a reaction to them — settling in, brightening, orienting. He's building a social world with the people in it. You're at the center.
Four months in. She is a different person than she was at birth and so are you. Neither of you is done becoming something, but what you already are together is already its own thing.
He sits with support now — propped on pillows or in your lap — and that changes what the world looks like to him. Everything is at a different angle. He's very interested in this new angle.
She may be rolling both directions now, or getting close. Once she can go both ways, she can start getting to things. Childproof the floor. She is more mobile than she looks.
He recognizes his name reliably now. Doesn't always respond to it — that comes later — but when you say it, something in him changes. He knows it's his.
She transfers objects hand to hand with intention. She'll look at something in her right hand, move it to her left, and look at it again like she's examining it from a new angle. She is.

He's starting to understand that other people have internal states. He watches your face when something happens — if there's a loud noise, he looks at you to figure out how to feel about it. You are his emotional reference point.
She may start to show a preference for certain people and a wariness toward strangers — not full-blown separation anxiety yet, but the beginning of it. She knows who she trusts. You're one of them.

Everything goes in his mouth. Not because he doesn't know better — it's how he understands objects right now. His mouth has more nerve endings than his hands. Mouthing is learning. Let him mouth things that are safe.

She's starting to sit for a few seconds without support. She'll wobble, she'll topple, she'll do it again. Keep pillows around her. Don't hold her upright — let her find her own balance, because that's what she's practicing.

He makes sounds that are starting to have the rhythm of conversation — turn-taking, pauses where he listens, then his turn again. He's practicing the structure of communication before he has any of the content.

She's aware of strangers in a new way this month. She may be fine with them or she may watch them carefully before deciding. Give her time to observe before putting her in a new person's arms. She's allowed to have this opinion.

He can find a partially hidden object. You put a toy under a blanket while he watches, leaving part of it visible, and he'll reach for the visible part. He's connecting what he sees to what must be there underneath.

She shows delight and she shows displeasure and she shows boredom and she shows curiosity and these are different states that you've learned to distinguish from one another. That's her emotional vocabulary emerging, and yours for reading it.

Tummy time on the floor is giving way to tummy time on purpose — he's pushing himself up to look at things, rolling toward things he wants, using his body with something like intention. He's becoming mobile in his own mind before his body catches up.
She may be starting to pull her feet toward her face. The foot will go in her mouth. This is fine. She's learning her own proportions.

He may start to protest when you take something away from him. That's new. It means he's developed enough object permanence to know that the thing still exists even though he can't see it anymore. He's upset because he knows it's there somewhere.

Five months is a good time to start simple routines that will last: a bath, a specific song, a few minutes of reading, a feed, sleep. The order matters more than the timing. She's starting to be able to anticipate what comes next.
He's going to be very interested in whatever you're doing. He'll want to touch your food, your phone, your face, your cup. He's learning by touching things. This is his research.
She may start to bounce rhythmically when she hears music. She's not dancing — she doesn't have the motor control — but her body is responding to rhythm. It's the beginning of something.

Solid foods are approaching. The signs of readiness: she can sit up with support, she's lost the tongue-thrust reflex, she shows interest in what you're eating. Don't act on those signs without talking to your pediatrician at the six-month visit.

He will drop things repeatedly from his high chair and watch them fall. This is not testing your patience — it's physics research. He's learning about gravity and cause and effect. He's also learning you'll pick things up, which is also useful information.

She may cry when you leave the room now in a way she didn't before. She knows you exist when you're not there, and she wants you there. Tell her you're leaving and that you'll be back. She won't understand the words yet, but the consistency of your coming back is the lesson.
He can push up to something close to sitting from tummy time now — not quite, but almost. The strength is there. The coordination is catching up.
She's starting to distinguish between familiar and unfamiliar voices. Not just by sound — by meaning. Your voice has a different effect than a stranger's voice even when the words are the same.

He may be teething now or he may not be for another month or two. The drooling, the chewing on everything, the fussiness — these show up before the tooth does. A cold teething ring helps. So does something firm to bite on with your fingers.

She's been alive for five months and she knows more than you know she knows. She remembers things. She recognizes places. She has expectations. All of that happened quietly while you were doing the daily work.
He is becoming a person with preferences and moods and a recognizable personality. That person was always in there. You've been meeting him gradually, one month at a time.
She responds to her name. Call it from across the room and she'll turn. That's not just hearing — that's identification. She knows that name means her.
He passes toys from one hand to the other, holds two things at once, drops one to grab a third. His hands are becoming instruments. He'll use them to learn everything that follows.

Around five months, many babies go through a phase of waking at night who had been sleeping better. It's not regression — it's developmental activity. Their brains are doing a lot and sleep cycles get disrupted. It passes.
Five months. She can sit. She can roll. She can reach and grab and hold. She knows you. She laughs. She studies faces. She has opinions. None of that existed when you brought her home.

Six months is a real milestone — not in the developmental checklist sense but in the 'you made it halfway through the first year' sense. It's harder than people told you and better than you expected. Both things are true.

She can sit without support for a few seconds now, maybe longer. She'll fall and sit again. The falling is part of it — her body is learning balance by losing it and recovering. Stay close but don't hold her up.
He strings vowel sounds together — 'aaaaah, ooooh, eeee' — longer and more varied than before. He's practicing the music of speech. Talk back in the same register. He loves the echo.

Solid foods start now if your pediatrician gives the go-ahead. First foods don't need to be rice cereal — you can start with pureed vegetables or fruits. Introduce one at a time, a few days apart, so you can notice if something doesn't agree with her.
She passes objects from hand to hand reliably now. She also puts everything in her mouth and then examines it afterward, as if the mouthing was data collection. It is.

He recognizes strangers as strangers. He may be fine with them or he may need time to warm up. Don't force the interaction. Let him set the pace. Stranger awareness is a developmental milestone, not a social problem.
She loves mirrors. She doesn't know the baby in the mirror is her — that understanding comes later — but she finds that baby very interesting and very friendly. Let her look.

He rocks back and forth on his hands and knees. He's not crawling yet — he's building the rocking motion that will become crawling. He may push himself backward before he goes forward. Backward first is normal.
Six-month vaccines happen now. If she's been on a roll developmentally, she may slow down for a few days afterward. The body is doing something else. Give her the rest.

He's starting to understand that your face gives him information about what's safe and what isn't. He'll look at you when something new happens. Your calm face tells him it's okay. Your alarmed face tells him something else. You're calibrating him.

She may get upset when you leave now in a way that felt gradual coming on but suddenly seems significant. Separation anxiety is a healthy developmental milestone, not something to fix. Say goodbye, mean it, come back.
He can roll in both directions now and cover more ground than you'd expect. The floor is his territory now. Anything on the floor is his to reach.

She responds to her own name reliably and to the names of people she knows. She looks when you say 'Daddy' or 'doggie' — she's building a vocabulary of names for things before she can say any of them.
He can hold and shake a rattle, hold two things at once, pass an object from one hand to the other. His hands are becoming capable. This is going to accelerate.

The first tooth may arrive around now, or it may not come for a few more months. The drooling and chewing have been going on for a while already. When a tooth does appear, run a clean finger over his gums gently after feedings.

Six months is a half-birthday worth acknowledging, even quietly. She's doubled in weight from birth. She can sit. She can eat. She has a personality you know. She knows you. Six months is significant.

He's showing emotions distinctly now — joy, frustration, surprise, fear, curiosity — and he's starting to show them in response to things that happen. He has feelings about the world. Name them for him even though he doesn't understand yet.
She may start to bang things — a block on the table, her hand on the tray, a spoon on anything. She's discovering that she can make sounds happen. That's cause and effect and it's thrilling to her.

He may roll from where he started all the way across the room. This is still how he gets places. Crawling is coming but the timeline varies enormously. Some babies skip crawling entirely and go straight to pulling up. The sequence matters less than the progress.

First foods are often a mess. She's learning to eat from a spoon, which is a whole skill she doesn't have yet. Most of it will end up on her face or the bib. That's fine. The quantity isn't the point at six months — the experience is.

He imitates sounds. You cough, he coughs. You click your tongue, he tries to. He's copying you and he's delighted when it works. This is how language will come — first the imitation of sound, then the imitation of words.
She can pivot in a circle on her belly now to reach things in different directions. She's problem-solving around her own physical limitations. She'll be mobile before long.

He may start to show distress when other children cry nearby. He's not empathetic in a cognitive sense yet, but emotional contagion is real and early. He's already affected by other people's feelings.
She may resist a nap she used to take. Some babies consolidate from three naps to two around six months. If a nap isn't happening despite clear tiredness, the nap schedule may need to shift.

He's starting to understand 'no' — not consistently, not reliably, but it registers. He'll pause. He may look at you. He may do the thing anyway. The understanding is there; the compliance comes much, much later.
She explores objects differently now — turning them over, feeling different sides, transferring hand to hand, mouthing and then looking. She's systematic. She's learning the properties of things.

He may be waking less at night than he was two months ago, or more. Six months is highly variable for sleep. Some babies settle here; some don't settle until nine months or later. Neither means you've done something wrong.
She has a laugh that's become specific to her. The things she finds funny are hers — they're not the same things another baby would find funny. She has a sense of humor that is already her own.
He can support his full weight on his legs when you hold him standing. He'll bounce. He'll push. He won't stand alone for a while yet, but his legs know what they're building toward.
Six months. The baby who came home is gone. The person who replaced her is more interesting and more work and you are more yourself than you were before she arrived.
He sits alone now. Not shakily — solidly, with his hands free to do things. That changes everything. The world he can access from sitting is enormous compared to what he could reach before.

She's starting to babble with consonants — 'ba, da, ma, ga' — in long strings. She'll say them to toys, to herself, to you, to the ceiling. She's not talking yet. She's practicing the physical work of talking.

He crawls now, or is close to it. Some babies do a belly crawl first. Some rock back and forth building up to it. A few go directly from sitting to pulling to stand. Whatever the sequence, he's working on getting somewhere.

Separation anxiety peaks somewhere between seven and twelve months. When she cries every time you leave the room, she's not being manipulative — she's showing you that she's developed the understanding that you exist when you're not there, and she wants you there. That's a milestone, even though it's hard.
He uses both hands together now — one to hold something stable, the other to explore it. He's coordinating two hands for one purpose. That requires more cognitive integration than it looks like.

She'll drop things off her high chair and watch them fall. Same game as last month. Still physics research. The game has a name in developmental science: she's testing object permanence. Does the thing still exist when she can't see it?

He moves objects in and out of containers. Puts something in, takes it out, puts it back. This is the forerunner of sorting, of spatial reasoning, of understanding that things fit into other things. It's a lot more than it looks.
She copies gestures now. Wave at her and she may wave back. Not always, not on command, but sometimes. That imitation is how she'll learn almost everything over the next two years.

He looks where you point. That's a significant cognitive development — he understands that your pointing finger indicates something elsewhere, and he follows the reference. Most animals can't do this. He can.

She's eating solid foods now and she may have preferences. She'll turn away from things she doesn't want. Respect it. Offer the rejected food again in a week or two. Tastes change, but forcing them doesn't help.

His stranger wariness is full on now. He may cry when unfamiliar people approach him too quickly. Give new people a way to warm up slowly — across the room first, then closer, let him reach toward them rather than putting him in their arms.
She can pull herself to sitting from lying down now. She's managing her own body in space in ways she couldn't a month ago.
He will pull himself to standing if he can reach furniture or your hand. He'll be thrilled about this. His legs are ready; his balance isn't yet. Stay close.

She claps now — or something that looks like clapping, with soft hands and uncertain timing. It doesn't matter. She figured out that her hands could meet and make noise. That's a small discovery with a very pleased baby behind it.

He's eating finger foods or getting close. Soft pieces he can hold and bring to his mouth himself. The goal of finger foods isn't nutrition — he's still getting that from milk. The goal is practicing the pincer grip and self-feeding.

She understands 'no' more consistently now, even though she may not always stop. Understanding and compliance are different skills. She's got the first one. The second takes longer and more repetition than feels reasonable.

He's forming strong attachments to specific people and specific objects. He may have a lovey now — a blanket, a stuffed animal — that helps him settle. Let him have it. It's not a crutch. It's a transitional object doing exactly what transitional objects are supposed to do.
She looks to you when something uncertain happens, checking your face for information. Your calm is data for her. Your alarm is also data. She's calibrating her responses to the world against yours.
He may be on two naps a day now — morning and afternoon — and sleeping better at night than he was a month ago. Or he may not be, and that's also within the range. Babies are variable.

She gets to objects by rolling, pivoting, scooting, or crawling. She has a destination. She has a strategy for reaching it. She has persistence when it doesn't work immediately. She is, at seven months, already someone who goes after what she wants.
He finds partially hidden toys. He'll lift a blanket to see what's under it. He knows there's something there — he just needs to find it. That's object permanence solidifying.

She may have one or two teeth now. The teething discomfort is real and intermittent — not constant. Hard things to chew on, cold things to mouth, and more holding on the hard days is the whole treatment.

He has a range of consonant-vowel combinations he uses expressively: 'dada' with frustration, 'mama' with wanting, 'baba' with something else. He doesn't mean 'mama' as a word for you yet — he's just using the sounds he has.

She's starting to have opinions about what she wants to eat and what she doesn't. If she's turning away from something, the hunger isn't there or the food isn't right. Don't add stress to mealtimes. Food should be neutral.

He may start to point at things — not to ask for them but to indicate them, to call your attention to something interesting. That pointing is one of the most significant developments of the whole first year. It's him starting to share experience with you deliberately.

Seven months is when life starts to require more active baby-proofing than you needed before. She's mobile. She is making her way toward the thing you didn't know you needed to move. Corners, electrical outlets, stairs.
He plays back and forth with you now — an object rolls to him, he rolls it back, or something close to that. Turn-taking in play is a skill and it's starting.
She may hold her own bottle or cup now. She'll want to. Let her try even though it takes longer and makes more mess. She needs the practice.

The changes this month are quieter than the big milestones of earlier months, but they're deep. The brain work happening at seven months is mostly invisible from the outside. Trust that it's happening even when the days feel still.
Seven months. He can get places, eat real food, sit by himself, and make sounds that are starting to mean something. He's not a newborn anymore in any sense. He's a person with skills.

She pulls to stand now. The first time she does it she'll look very pleased. The problem is getting down — she hasn't figured that out yet. She'll cry from standing. Show her how to bend her knees and sit back down.
He crawls — forward this time, with intention. He has places to go. The house looks completely different to you now. Everything on the floor is his.
She uses her index finger to point at things, poke at things, press buttons on things. The index finger is becoming a tool. That's refined motor control, and it's new.

He has a pincer grip now or is developing it — thumb and forefinger picking up small things. This is the manual dexterity that will eventually allow him to hold a pencil, button a shirt, do surgery if he wants to. It starts with picking up peas.

She understands 'no' and 'come here' and her name and a handful of other words. Her receptive vocabulary — what she understands — is outrunning her expressive vocabulary by a lot. She knows far more than she can say.

He points to show you things. Not to ask for them — to share them. He sees something interesting and he wants you to see it too. That shared attention is the beginning of communication as we actually use it.

She's aware of her own reflection now, and there's something in her that recognizes it more than she recognizes a random face. She's not there yet — full self-recognition in a mirror doesn't come until 18 months — but she's tracking toward it.
He may cruise along furniture now — holding on and moving sideways, legs working, hands moving from grip to grip. He's walking. He just hasn't let go yet.

She may be down to two naps that are becoming more predictable — mid-morning and mid-afternoon. If she seems well-rested and fighting a nap, the schedule may need to shift slightly. Bodies change what they need.
He imitates actions now — banging, waving, patting, shaking. He sees you do something and he tries it. That imitation is his primary learning mechanism right now. Everything you do is a lesson.
She responds to her name and to simple phrases she hears often. When you say 'bath time' she may start moving toward the bathroom. She's connecting your words to the things that follow them.
He can feed himself soft finger foods pretty reliably now. Pieces of banana, soft cooked vegetables, small bits of cheese. His diet is expanding. The mess is part of it.

She looks for something you've hidden from her. The object exists in her mind even when she can't see it. She'll search. She may look in the wrong place at first — she hasn't fully worked out that things can only be in one place at a time.
He may say 'mama' or 'dada' with something close to meaning now — using it toward the right person more often than not. He's connecting sounds to people. That's the first step of language.
She has consistent preferences now — preferred foods, preferred toys, preferred people, preferred positions. She knows what she likes. This will become her character.

He may start to show frustration when he can't do something — reaching for something out of range, or trying to open something he can't open. That frustration is the precursor of persistence. It means he cares about doing the thing.
She waves goodbye now, sometimes spontaneously. She doesn't fully understand what it means — she'll wave when no one is leaving — but she knows it's a social gesture and she's practicing it.
He drinks from a cup with help. The transition from bottle to cup is long and the cup will win eventually. The earlier the cup becomes familiar, the easier the transition will be.
She can clap her hands together in response to something exciting now. The clapping has become expressive. She's not just doing it — she's doing it because something pleased her.

He has the beginnings of object categorization. He knows that certain things go together — that blocks are for stacking, that spoons are for eating, that a book opens. He's building schemas for how the world is organized.
She pushes away things she doesn't want. She turns her face from food she's finished with. She hands you the toy when she's done with it. She's communicating through her body very efficiently.

He may go through a phase of night waking again around eight months. It coincides with big developmental changes — standing, cruising, expanded cognition — that can disrupt sleep. Knowing why doesn't make three AM easier but it makes it less alarming.

She plays peek-a-boo with full understanding now. She knows you're there behind your hands. She's laughing at the game, not at the surprise — she anticipates the reveal. That's different from four months ago.
He looks before he reaches — his eyes arrive somewhere before his hands do. The visual planning that preceded the physical action is getting more sophisticated.
She may start to push a toy in front of her and use it to help herself walk. She'll go places she couldn't reach before. The entire house is now hers to explore.

He may have specific fears now — the vacuum cleaner, the bath drain, a certain face. Don't dismiss these. They're real to him, and dismissing them teaches him his perception doesn't matter. Acknowledge the fear and stay close.

She uses two hands for two different tasks — one holding, one exploring. Her brain is coordinating more complex bilateral activity. That kind of coordination is a prerequisite for everything she'll learn to do with her hands over the next decade.
He imitates sounds he hears in conversation — not words yet, but the melody and cadence of speech. He's learning what talking sounds like from the inside of a conversation he's having.
Eight months is a full one. Standing, cruising, pointing, imitating, understanding words, pincer grip, object permanence. Each of those is a major development. They all came in about thirty days.
She is a crawler, a stander, a talker-in-her-own-way, a person with preferences and moods and people she loves. She didn't exist eight months ago. She's been doing this while you watched.

The nine-month visit is one of the more important well-child visits. Come with questions. Your pediatrician will ask about language, about motor development, about feeding. This is a good time to say anything that's been on your mind.

She may say 'mama' or 'dada' with clear meaning now — using the right name for the right person most of the time. That's her first real word, or very close to it. It will happen more than once before you're sure it's intentional, and then you'll be sure.

He understands 'no' reliably. He still may not stop — he's learning the concept, not the compliance. The compliance takes time and repetition and patience and more patience. But the understanding is there.

She points to things she wants, to things she finds interesting, to things she wants you to look at. She's doing three different kinds of pointing with three different purposes. That's sophisticated for nine months.
He claps when he's pleased. He waves when someone leaves. He shakes his head to mean no. He's using gestures as intentional communication, not just imitation. He has things to say.

She may be pulling to stand, cruising along furniture, and maybe — briefly — standing with nothing to hold on to before sitting back down. The standing without support will come soon. The walking shortly after. Not yet, but soon.

He puts things in containers and takes them out. This sounds like nothing. It's spatial reasoning, hand-eye coordination, cause and effect, and executive function all at once. He'll do it for a long time because there's a lot to learn from it.

Separation anxiety may peak now. She knows you exist when you're gone and she prefers you to be there. Say goodbye clearly and come back reliably. She needs the going and the returning to be consistent.
He understands object permanence fully now. He'll look for something you hid even when he didn't see where you hid it. He's developed a theory of where things might be. That's inference.

She feeds herself finger foods reliably. The mess has become part of the ritual. She eats some things and rejects others. Keep offering variety. Rejected foods often become accepted foods after eight to ten exposures.

He uses sounds and gestures together now — pointing and vocalizing at the same time, or reaching and making a particular sound that means 'I want that.' He's communicating in sentences before he has words.
She may be moving toward one long nap instead of two. Many babies make this transition between nine and eighteen months. If the morning nap is becoming a battle, the consolidation may be starting.

He copies what you do with objects — he picks up a phone and holds it to his ear, he picks up a spoon and tries to eat with it. He knows what things are for. That's functional play and it just started.

She looks where you look when you look at something and say something about it. That's joint attention — she's following your gaze to understand what you're referring to. It's the foundation of language comprehension.

He has strong attachments to specific comfort objects now, and they matter. The blanket, the stuffed animal, whatever it is — it helps him self-regulate. If it goes missing, replace it with effort. It matters to him in a real way.

She shows things to you — brings you a toy to show you, holds up something she found, displays something she accomplished. She wants you to see what she sees. That sharing is one of the roots of connection between people.

He understands more words than you know he does. If you mention bath and he starts moving toward the bathroom, if you say 'where's the dog' and he looks for the dog — he has a receptive vocabulary that's bigger than it appears.
She's getting good at feeding herself. Let her. It's slow and messy but the practice is the point. Independence around food that begins now will matter for a long time.
He may stand briefly without holding on — a few seconds before sitting back down. When it happens, it feels sudden. He's been building toward it all along.

She tests limits. She does the thing and looks at you. She's not being difficult — she's doing research on the rules of her world. What happens when she does this? What happens when she does it again? Your consistency is the answer.

He's attached to specific people and can show it clearly — reaching for you specifically, preferring certain people over others, being distressed by people he doesn't know well. This selectivity is healthy.

She uses babbling that sounds like sentences — the rhythm and intonation of speech without the actual words. She'll 'talk' at length. It sounds like another language, because it is — the shape of language before content fills it in.
He finds things you've hidden by looking in the right places based on where you went. He's tracking your movement as information. He's figured out that the thing is where you were.

She drinks from a cup more reliably now. A sippy cup or an open cup with help — both are fine. The goal is not the cup type; the goal is getting comfortable with a cup before the first birthday, when milk volume will start to decrease.

Nine months is the developmental halfway point of the first year. Your baby at nine months is more similar to your baby at twelve months than he is to your baby at six months. The pace of change is shifting.

She has about four to six clear gestures — pointing, waving, clapping, reaching up to be held, shaking her head no. Those gestures are language. They count. Some children use gestures long after they also have words.

He pushes back when he doesn't want something. He turns away from a food, pushes a toy aside, makes his body rigid when he doesn't want to be held. He's expressing preference with his whole body. That's legitimate communication.
She's nine months old, which means she's been in the world as long as she was inside it. Some people find that remarkable. It is.
The connection between the two of you at nine months is different from what it was at one month, or at six. It has a history now. She knows things about you that she's never told anyone.

Nine months. He walks along furniture, eats real food, understands dozens of words, points at the things that interest him, and knows who the people in his life are. He's been doing all of this in front of you.

She may take her first steps this month. Or she may not, and walk at twelve months, or fourteen. The range for first independent steps is wide. When it happens it will be two or three steps before she sits down, and it will feel enormous.
He stands alone for several seconds now. He practices without thinking about it — stands up, balances, sits back down, stands again. The repetition is how the balance system calibrates itself.
She uses 'mama' and 'dada' correctly and may have one or two other words. The words are often not clear to anyone outside your household. That's fine. You're the right audience for first words.
He responds to simple questions — 'Where is the ball?' — by looking at or reaching for the right thing. He understands far more than he can say, which will be true for the next year.

She has preferences about how she's dressed, what she eats, where she goes, who holds her. She makes them known. This is not willfulness — it's the emergence of self. It will intensify. Knowing that helps.

He stacks blocks — two at a time, maybe three. He knocks them down. He stacks them again. The stacking and the knocking down are equally important to him. He's learning about towers and gravity and his own power over things.
She waves goodbye reliably and appropriately. She gives objects to people and takes them back. The social reciprocity — the back-and-forth of objects and attention — is becoming a fluent thing.
He may have a word for 'more' — the sign for it, or a sound he makes consistently when he wants more food. Functional communication about wants is arriving.
She's starting to use objects as tools — using one thing to get another, or using a stick to push something out of reach. Basic tool use. It's the beginning of a very long line of problem-solving.
He understands 'give it to me' and 'put it down' and several other simple commands if they're said consistently. He may not always comply, but he knows what they mean.

She points to pictures in books and looks at you expectantly when you name them. She's making connections between printed images and real objects. She's starting to understand that pictures represent things.

He has a recognizable style of play — he lines things up, or he explores methodically, or he's physical and kinetic, or he narrates everything with sounds. His play style is already a version of his personality.
She takes one or two steps now and then, usually without realizing she's doing it. She's not thinking 'I will take steps.' Her legs are just doing things sometimes.
He drinks from a cup independently. He may still want a bottle at certain times — the bottle is not just nutrition, it's comfort. But the cup is becoming something he can manage on his own.

She has a consistent bedtime routine by now, or she should. Bath, a few minutes of reading, the same song, the same sequence. The routine isn't about making her sleep — it's about signaling that sleep is coming. The signal becomes the thing that helps.
Three hundred days. He has been alive for three hundred days. The person he is now was entirely made in that time. That's worth sitting with for a moment.
She uses gestures alongside sounds to communicate — pointing and saying 'da' to mean 'look at that.' The combination of gesture and sound is more sophisticated communication than either alone.
He explores cause and effect deliberately now. He does something to see what happens. He does it again to confirm. He changes one thing to see if the outcome changes. He's running experiments.

She may have six to eight teeth now, or fewer — teething is highly variable. She'll have all twenty primary teeth by around age three, on her own schedule. The timing of tooth arrival doesn't mean anything.
He understands the names of the people he sees regularly. Say 'Where's Daddy?' and he'll look for Daddy. He has a mental map of the people in his world with names attached.

She may be trying to scribble if she gets her hands on a crayon. Let her. The marks don't mean anything yet — she's learning that her hand can make something on paper. That's the whole lesson for now.

He may refuse certain foods for a while and then accept them again without any change in how you offered them. The palate is developing. A food that seemed rejected may just need fifteen more introductions.

She dances when she hears music — bouncing, swaying, sometimes waving her arms. She's responding to rhythm with her whole body. Music will be something she uses to regulate herself for the rest of her life, and it starts now.

He may say three or four words now, or none yet. First words range from ten months to sixteen months and the range is completely normal. What matters more than words at this age is whether he's communicating — with sounds, gestures, looks, and pointing.
She's practicing walking by holding one of your hands and walking alongside you. She leans into you, she trusts you to catch her. That trust runs deeper than the walking.

He identifies objects in pictures and may name some of them — 'dog,' 'ball,' 'cat' — with something like the right sound even if it's not the full word. 'Ba' for ball. 'Ga' for dog. He knows what things are called.
She helps you dress her. She puts her arm through the sleeve when you hold it, lifts her foot for the shoe. That participation is the beginning of independence around the daily routines.
He has a sense of humor. He does things he finds funny, looks to see if you're laughing, does it again if you are. He's performing. He's reading his audience. He's eleven months old.

She's almost one. The person she is at almost-one is someone you know. You know what she finds funny, what frightens her, what she reaches for, what makes her settle. That knowledge took a year to build.
In the next few weeks she'll walk, or she already has. Either way, something shifts when a baby walks. They become more separate. That's the whole point. You've been helping her get there.

One year old. You did that. You and her, together — three hundred and sixty-five days of figuring it out. Nothing about that year was what you expected, and nothing about it was what you should have been told to expect. You lived it instead.
She may be walking now — a few steps, then more — or she may walk in the next few weeks. The range is ten to fourteen months and all of it is normal. Walking comes when it comes.

He has two to three clear words by now, or he's working toward it. A word counts when he uses it consistently to mean the same thing — 'ba' for ball every time he sees a ball. Consistency is the signal.

She feeds herself almost entirely with her hands and is working on a spoon. The spoon will take a while. It requires rotating the wrist in a specific way that's harder than it looks. Let her practice even when it's slow.

He has strong opinions about who holds him, what he eats, what he does next. This is going to intensify considerably over the next year. You're at the beginning of what people call the toddler phase, which starts before two.

The one-year well visit includes some important things: developmental screening, first influenza vaccine if not already given, lead screening, and an assessment of language and communication. Come with anything that's been on your mind.

She points to things and says a sound that means 'what is that?' She wants names for things now. She's building vocabulary through exactly this mechanism — asking, hearing, repeating. Name things for her all the time.

He drinks whole cow's milk now, or non-dairy equivalent, if your pediatrician has given the go-ahead. The transition from formula or breast milk to cow's milk happens around the first birthday. Ask at the twelve-month visit about timing and amounts.
She says 'no' — verbally or with her head shake — and means it. Respecting her 'no' in age-appropriate contexts is not giving in to a toddler. It's teaching her that her communication works.
He waves, he claps, he plays pat-a-cake, he gives and takes objects in game-like sequences. Social play is well-established. He knows he's in a relationship with you.

She walks holding onto furniture or your hand, and possibly alone. When she walks alone, she'll often look at her feet and fall. When she stops looking at her feet, she'll walk more steadily. The attention has to go somewhere else.
He finds things hidden in two places now — he knows the object had to go somewhere, and he checks the right somewhere. His model of the physical world is getting sophisticated.
She puts things in and takes things out of containers with speed and intention. She stacks two blocks, knocks them down, stacks them again. The manipulation of objects is becoming purposeful.
He uses one hand more than the other now. That hand preference will solidify over the next year. Whatever hand it is, it's the right one for him.
She pokes at things with her finger — the screen, a picture in a book, a bug she's found on the floor. She's investigating. The index finger is her primary research instrument.

He may have a tantrum now, or close to it — frustration that exceeds his ability to express it, and so his body takes over. This will get more frequent before it gets less frequent. It's not a behavior problem. It's an emotion regulation problem that will improve as language catches up.
She imitates adult activities with her whole body — sweeping, rocking a doll, talking on the phone. That pretend play is sophisticated. She knows what these actions mean.

He has a clear sense of himself as separate from you. He's been building this understanding all year. At one year, he knows he is a person and you are a different person. That's a real cognitive achievement.
She shows what she wants by pointing, reaching, vocalizing, and looking at you to check if you understood. She has a whole communication system that doesn't require words. The words are coming.

At twelve months, the number of new words she adds will start to accelerate. It won't feel sudden — it will feel like one word, then another, then another — and then one day you'll realize she has a vocabulary.

He is in many ways the same person you'll know at four, at eight, at twenty. The temperament, the way he looks at things, the quality of his curiosity — those are his. You're watching someone become themselves.
She may seem like she's forgotten a skill she had and then do it again a week later. That's not regression — that's how learning works. Skills consolidate with dips. The dips are part of the process.

He understands 'hot,' 'careful,' 'gentle,' 'come,' 'give me,' 'no,' and many more. His receptive vocabulary at one year is somewhere around fifty words. His expressive vocabulary is a few. That gap will close but it takes time.

She looks at books with you and points to pictures and makes the sounds of animals and objects she recognizes. That shared book time is building something — attention span, vocabulary, the understanding that pictures and words go together.
He can walk alone, or will soon. When he goes, he'll go with his hands up for balance and his feet wide apart and he'll look very serious about it. Let him go. Fall down is part of the method.
She has a person she prefers above all others. Possibly you, possibly someone else, possibly she has two people at the top. Either way, those attachments are healthy and secure and you built them.

He knows his name and responds to it. He knows the names of the people he loves. He knows a dozen object names. He knows words for some actions. He knows words for some feelings. He is using language even before he speaks it.
One year ago you met each other. Everything you know about her you learned in the last twelve months. And there's a whole life ahead of both of you.

The first year is over. The second begins. The things that were hard are different now. The things that were easy are different now. You know more than you knew, and there's more to learn, and that's true of every year that follows.

You did a year. Whatever help you had or didn't have, whatever it cost you, whatever you got wrong and what you got right — you were there for every day of it. That's the only thing that matters, and you did it.
